newsitem.title: LEBANON: FEATURE - Lebanese banks seek $1 billion on euromarket.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Lebanese banks seek $1 billion on euromarket.

text.p: Lebanon's top banks, which began tapping the international debt market in June, have raised $320 million so far and more issues are expected in the coming months.

The government is encouraging the banks to seek finance abroad to counter slowing inflows of capital, a shortage of liquidity in the economy, slowing growth and the spectre of a balance of payments deficit, bankers and economists say.
Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri is urging the banks to raise $800-$1 billion abroad by mid-1997, they add.
Credit Libanais, owned by the central bank, launched a $60 million eurobond in June -- the first by a Lebanese bank.

In September, Byblos Bank issued a $50 million eurobond, Hariri's Banque Mediterranee followed with a $100 million EuroCD and Banque Beyrouth pour le Commerce raised a $12 million EuroCD. In October, Banque Audi issued a $100 million eurobond.
The government and the banks have converging interests in seeking medium- and long-term money abroad.

Lebanese banks are branching out into consumer financing -- credit cards, mortgages and car loans -- and project financing but are hampered by persistent dependence on short-term deposits averaging 45-50 days and by a slowdown this year in deposits growth.
A NEED FOR LONG-TERM FUNDS

"The main shortage in the system is long- and medium-term funds. The banks want longer maturities to match the uses of funds which they are developing," Marwan Ghandour, chairman of Lebanon Invest finance house which helped manage the Byblos issue, told Reuters.
"Some 80 percent or so of all borrowing here is in dollars," Ghandour added. "So the oil that fuels the economy is dollars and they need these dollar revenues to fuel economic activity."
Mustapha Razian, chairman of Banque Mediterranee, Lebanon's biggest bank which specialises in project financing, says it is about time Lebanon's banks tapped the international market.
"The deposit base of the Lebanese public is very much constrained," said Razian.
"Growth is slowing and most Lebanese money is already invested, so the only way for the private sector to grow and to finance infrastructure projects is to tap the international market," he said.
Razian said Hariri's target of $1 billion was realistic but perhaps not by mid-1997, because only a handful of Lebanon's 82 banks were in a position to go to the international market.
"It may take longer. By the end of next year I think the industry will have raised $1 billion." he said.

Mediterranee itself plans to raise another $200 million in EuroCDs, part of it before the end of the year, Razian said. A $150 million issue of Global Depository Receipts (GDR) planned by Lebanon's biggest company SOLIDERE will also boost the inflow.
Despite the success of the issues so far, Razian said most of the funds they were attracting was expatriate capital.
"Most of the subscribers to these issues are Lebanese nationals," he said. "These instruments are encouraging Lebanese abroad with funds in foreign banks to invest in Lebanon."
Charles Samen of Banque Paribas' emerging markets in London agreed that most of the money being attracted was traditionally from the diaspora and Middle Eastern institutions.

"But it is notable that we are seeing increased interest and name recognition from institutional investors in Europe who are seeking to expand on their holdings and this will result in an increasingly diversified placement of future issues," he said.
BALANCE OF PAYMENTS WORRIES
According to Lebanese economist Marwan Iskander, balance of payments concerns and a need to stimulate the economy are the government's main interests in urging the banks to go abroad.
"They (the government) realise the capital inflow is no longer what it was -- that's why they are trying to fill the gap," Iskander told Reuters.
He estimated that inflows may fall to $4.8-$5 billion this year from $6 billion in 1994 -- partly because of a fall-off in Lebanon's real estate boom which has attracted large sums.

This is causing government anxiety about the balance of payments, which dropped in 1995 to a $256 million surplus from $1.13 billion in 1994 and but for a $300 million government eurobond would have been in deficit, Iskander said.
"For 1997 and the rest of 1996 the government and central bank feel it is essential to have a balance of payments surplus," he said.

However, the government cannot return to the international market because its $900 million foreign borrowing authorisation from parliament is exhausted. It has raised $800 million in eurobonds since October 1994 and is preparing a new $100 million issue.
Foreign debt is a prickly political issue in Lebanon and it is not known when Hariri may ask the new parliament elected in September for further authorisation.

His government has accumulated $1.5 billion in external debt as it struggles to rebuild the country, and total public debt has soared above 16 trillion Lebanese pounds ($10.5 billion) -- more than 90 percent of GDP.
The government also hopes the foreign funds will stimulate the private sector which is being crowded out by high interest rates on treasury bills -- the government's main debt-financing instrument.
Economic growth has slowed sharply this year and is expected to be about half the 1995 rate of seven percent.
